To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

Korean expatriates working in China have a more positive attitude than Chinese workers towards training methods that focus on the importance of the training to their job performance and career success, and on training that allows learners to control their own learning process, while the Chinese workers have a more positive view of training methods that focus more on the training itself and on the training climate.

Korean expatriates working in China and Chinese employees in the PRC have different perceptions of the importance of training methods, but both groups agree that training methods should be linked to career success and should give learners control over their learning process.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the congruence or lack thereof between the perceptions of Korean multinational managers and Chinese workers on the importance of training methods.
how multinational corporations can effectively train and develop their Chinese employees.
the issue of training approach congruence between Korean expatriates (multinational managers) and Chinese host country nationals in the PRC.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Korean expatriate and Chinese host country national employee perceptions of training approach importance do not converge on all measures.
Korean expatriates are not as effective as they could be in training Chinese workers.
there are significant differences in the perceptions of Korean expatriates versus Chinese employees regarding training methods, but that there is also a significant degree of congruence.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Korean and PRC workers are not in agreement on the importance of training method, but are congruent on the two dimensions of ‘link’ and ‘control’.
multinational organizations should be aware of the importance of training for Chinese employees.
Korean expatriates are more likely than PRC employees to view the importance of training in terms of the ‘career success’ dimension.
The main takeaway from our work is that

multinational firms must take into account both the convergence and divergence of host country national and expatriate workforce perceptions when designing and delivering training to enhance global productivity.
Korean expatriate managers should be aware of their Chinese subordinates’ perceptions regarding training and should be sensitive in their efforts to implement training programs in China.

multinational firms should be aware of the need to adapt training approaches to the local workforce, but that the need to provide effective training is more important than the specific training approach.
